title: March C− and proving coverage
summary: **March C−** is the best-known March test: 10N operations that detect all stuck-at, address-decoder, transition and unlinked coupling faults. This topic walks through its six elements and shows how to **prove** that a test detects a fault model — case by case.
objectives: Write March C− and explain the role of each of its six elements.
Prove that a March test detects a fault by following all aggressor/victim cases.
Explain why removing an element makes some faults escape.

blocks.md:
> **March C−** = {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇑(r1, w0); ⇓(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0); ⇕(r0)}  — **10N**

The pattern is easy to remember: after initialising, the test does **both transitions going up**, then **both transitions going down**, and finishes with a read.

steps.title: M0 ⇕(w0)
steps.md: Initialise every cell to 0. Nothing is checked yet.

steps.title: M1 ⇑(r0, w1)
steps.md: Going up: check the 0, then make the **0 → 1** transition. Aggressors **below** a victim change before the victim is read.

steps.title: M2 ⇑(r1, w0)
steps.md: Going up again: check the 1, make the **1 → 0** transition.

steps.title: M3 ⇓(r0, w1)
steps.md: Going **down**: now aggressors **above** a victim change before the victim is read.

steps.title: M4 ⇓(r1, w0)
steps.md: Going down with the opposite transition.

steps.title: M5 ⇕(r0)
steps.md: A final read of every cell. It catches what the last writes of M4 did to cells that M4 had already passed.

rows: ✓ all — M1 and M4 form the AF condition
✓ all, when they are not linked
blocks.caption: What March C− covers

blocks.title: March C and March C−
blocks.md: The original **March C** (Marinescu, 1982) had one more element, an extra ⇕(r0) in the middle — **11N**. Van de Goor showed that for the classical fault models this read adds nothing, and removed it: **March C−**, 10N.

How do we *know* March C− detects every idempotent coupling fault (CFid)? We check **every case**. A CFid has a trigger (↑ or ↓ in the aggressor), a forced value (0 or 1 in the victim) and a position (aggressor below or above the victim) — **2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cases**.

Worked example **⟨↑;0⟩, a < v**: the fault only shows if v holds **1** when a rises.

1. M1 ⇑: a rises — but v is not visited yet and still holds 0. Forcing 0 changes nothing.
2. M2 ⇑: a falls — no trigger.
3. M3 ⇓: going **down**, v is visited first and becomes 1. Then a rises → v is forced to **0**.
4. M4 ⇓: going down, v is read first: expected 1, read **0** → **detected in M4**.

blocks.caption: The element where each of the 8 CFid cases is detected (checked with a fault simulator)

blocks.title: Every case has an entry — so the proof is complete
blocks.md: If one cell of the table said *escape*, the test would not cover the fault model. This case-by-case method is how every coverage claim in the literature is made — today usually with a **fault simulator** that runs the test on a memory model with each fault injected.

items.title: Remove M5 ⇕(r0)
items.md: Look at the table: ⟨↓;1⟩ with a < v is detected **only** in M5. Without M5, about one in eight CFid cases escapes (in a simulation of a 6-cell memory, 15 of 120 CFid faults).

items.title: Make M3 and M4 go up instead of down
items.md: Then the test never lets an aggressor *above* the victim act before the victim is read in the right state. In simulation **half** of all CFid faults escape.

items.title: Remove M4 (and end with ⇕(r1))
items.md: Going down, the test now makes only the 0 → 1 transition. The 1 → 0 transitions of aggressors above a victim are never checked — in simulation **a quarter** of the CFid faults (30 of 120) escape.

items.title: Add more elements
items.md: Extra reads or writes cost time but can catch more fault models — that is the subject of the next topic (DRDF, WDF, linked faults).

blocks.prompt: Practice: put the elements of March C− in order.

questions.text: Put the elements of March C− in order.
In March C−, a CFid ⟨↑;1⟩ with the aggressor **below** the victim: where is it detected?
questions.explain: Going up, the aggressor rises before the victim is visited and forces it to 1; M1 then reads the victim expecting 0.

questions.text: How many cases must be checked to prove that a test detects all CFid faults?
